title: Supply-side policies
summary: Supply-side policies aim to raise long-run productive capacity, shifting LRAS right. Market-based policies rely on freer markets; interventionist policies use government investment. They take time and have costs.

keyterms.definition: Policies aimed at increasing the quantity or quality of factors of production, shifting LRAS right.
Policies that improve how markets work: deregulation, privatisation, competition policy, tax cuts and labour market reforms.
Government investment in education, training, healthcare, infrastructure, research and industrial policy.
Removing or reducing rules that restrict competition or raise costs for firms.
Selling state-owned firms to the private sector to increase efficiency through the profit motive.
Laws and agencies that prevent anti-competitive behaviour such as cartels and abuse of monopoly power.
Measures making labour markets more flexible, e.g. reducing trade union power or minimum wage, or easing hiring and firing.
Physical capital such as roads, ports, broadband and power networks that support production.
The skills, knowledge and health of workers, which raise their productivity.
Government support for specific sectors, e.g. subsidies or tax credits for green technology or R&D.
Output per worker or per hour worked.

questions.prompt: What is the main aim of supply-side policies?
options: To cut the budget deficit immediately
To raise potential output by shifting LRAS right
questions.explanation: They target the economy’s productive capacity.
Market-based policies reduce government role; interventionist ones increase it.

questions.statement: Spending on education is an interventionist supply-side policy that raises human capital.
questions.explanation: Better skills raise productivity, though benefits take years.

questions.text: Selling state-owned firms to private owners is ___.
questions.explanation: The aim is efficiency through the profit motive and competition.

questions.prompt: Which is a labour market reform?
options: Reducing restrictions on hiring and firing
questions.explanation: Such reforms aim to make labour markets more flexible.

questions.prompt: How can investment in infrastructure shift LRAS?
options: Lower transport costs and better connectivity raise productivity
questions.explanation: Infrastructure also adds to AD in the short run when it is built.

questions.statement: Competition policy aims to protect cartels from new entrants.
questions.explanation: It prevents anti-competitive behaviour such as cartels and abuse of dominance.
Higher productivity is the source of long-run growth in living standards.

questions.prompt: A government gives tax credits to firms developing battery technology. This is…
questions.explanation: Industrial policy targets particular sectors.

questions.prompt: Order how a training programme raises growth.
questions.explanation: Interventionist policies raise human capital.

questions.prompt: Which is a major limitation of supply-side policies?
options: They take a long time to have an effect
questions.explanation: Education and infrastructure take years to raise capacity.

questions.statement: Supply-side policies can reduce inflation and unemployment at the same time in the long run.
questions.explanation: Shifting LRAS right raises output while easing price pressure.

questions.prompt: Which is a criticism of labour market reforms such as cutting the minimum wage?
options: They may increase inequality and in-work poverty
questions.explanation: Flexibility may come at the cost of equity.

questions.prompt: Which policy affects BOTH AD and LRAS?
questions.explanation: Spending raises AD now; the finished infrastructure raises capacity later.

questions.text: Removing rules that restrict competition is called ___.
questions.explanation: Deregulation aims to lower costs and encourage entry.

questions.prompt: Match each policy to a key weakness.
questions.explanation: No single policy is best; a mix is usually used.
A private monopoly may simply exploit market power; regulation and competition still matter.

questions.prompt: An economy has high structural unemployment. Which policy mix is most suitable?
options: Retraining schemes and support for labour mobility
questions.explanation: Structural problems need supply-side solutions.

questions.text: Policies that improve how markets work, such as tax cuts and deregulation, are ___-based.
questions.explanation: They rely on incentives and competition.

questions.prompt: Order a strong 15-mark evaluation of a supply-side policy.
items: Define the policy and explain how it works
Illustrate with an AD/AS diagram showing LRAS shifting
Weigh time lags, costs and stakeholders
questions.explanation: Evaluation needs balance, context and a clear judgement.
